Very competitive course, I revise so hard and only got mean score

Exams basically ask you what the experimental results are, such as what is the reaction time needed for the scenario above, so memorise the result in as much detail as possible. sections.content:
Easy and interesting content, similar to the course content of cognitive psychology for the first phase of learning.

The course is divided into two modules, Limits in Human Cognition and Common Biases in Judgment and Decision Making.

Limits in Human Cognition part is kinda boring cuz it is somehow the same as cognitive psychology which I have learned before, but still fun if you have never studied cognitive psychology before.

Common Biases in Judgment and Decision Making seem to be more interesting, there are many examples given by the instructor, which are quite fun and enhanced our understanding on the corresponding biases. For the common biases part there are 7 different topics included, with the basic introduction and the underlying mechanisms of the bias.

sections.teaching: Carmen is one of the best profs I have met, she is very helpful by giving lots of honest feedbacks, also replying emails quickly which obviously helps a lot. She will arrange a revision session before each exam to answer students' question about exam contents. A project consultation session is also arranged for each project group to make sure their topics are related and relevant to the course. Every lecture will have small experiments which engage students to participate, the class atmosphere was really great!!
sections.grading:
The course basically is graded based on:
Exam 1 & 2 (~60% combined)
Project report presentation (30%)
Participation (~10%)
Both my exams were just under the mean, I was at the mean for the project report and presentation, and I got high marks in participation. In the end I got B range, which is surprising as I thought I would get C range in a SBM course (yes, I'm from SENG).
sections.workload:
The workload (listed in the Grading section on the left) was decent for a 3-credit course for me.

Its technically not a midterm and final exam because they were a bit earlier than the usual midterm/ final period. Obviously you have to pay attention to the examples and experiments in lectures to get high score in exams. And the exams were all MC questions.

For the presentation, as long as you get good teammates (not freeriders) it honestly wasn't a lot of work to do, in fact it was quite fun throughout the project period.

As for the participation part, you just need to answer Carmen's questions in lectures (best to answer in every lecture) and also ask questions to other groups during their presentation, then you should get most if not full mark here.

sections.content:

Her teaching is simple yet interesting. In each class, she will prepare handouts for students, give sufficient example to explain the theories and how it can be avoided or apply to daily lives. She will also share some interesting findings from data collected in class.
Project consultation session will be arranged before group presentation, feedback will be given after presentation to improve the final report.

Only simple exercise are given for practising the exam. No quizzes, essay or reading material for the class so it is easy to manage. However, attendance will be taken in each class.

You'll have a consultation meeting with Prof. Ng where she'll help guide you through and make sure you're on the right path so the project was pretty manageable(given you have responsible teammates).

Exams ask all numerical questions and it is not difficult to answer as far as you have attended the class. Full mark is 75 and mean is usually ~60. Standard deviation is ~10.
There is no step points and each question takes nearly 10 marks.

The group project ask you to Identify and describe of an important real‐world issue, and to apply the concepts learnt in class to solve it. You can form groups by yourself.
sections.workload: There is no homework at all. Before the presentation workload is almost zero.
